title: Studio reads one Clock, and a test holds it still

statements.says: Studio reads one Clock: everything that needs now, a wait or a delay reads it.
A test holds the Clock still and moves it on purpose.
A Patience, the wait on a store, is measured on the Clock inside the reader that waits.
The rule is written down in a rules file named for determinism rather than for time.
The C# half of the check lives in the Architecture project, which parses C# and so never matches a file name or a string.
The TypeScript half of the check lives in the front end's own linter, beside the module boundaries it already holds.
A reach for the machine's clock is a breach in shipping code and in a test, and is allowed in a Support file.
Ordering, identifiers and culture get sections in the determinism file when they are settled, rather than files of their own.
The wait on a store is called Patience, not Timeout.
The still Clock is the one Microsoft ships, not one written in the repo.
The front end gains a Clock of its own, supplied the way the C# one is.
The real store containers stay, and a fake belongs only where the real thing cannot be made to misbehave or where it forces a race.
Three stores set client.Timeout, which HttpClient measures on the machine's clock whatever Clock is injected, so the test Clock had to run at real speed for a wait to end.
With the test Clock at real speed, whether a read fell short depended on what else the machine was doing, and tests failed a different one each run under load.
A Support file may reach the machine's clock because a poll that waits for a container to be ready has to live somewhere.
The file is named for determinism because an agent is non-deterministic by construction and steering it away from non-determinism is a standing need.
Holding time still turns a test that races by construction, such as one using a real delay to outlast a wait, into a test that fails every run until it moves the Clock on purpose.
The front end needs a Clock because two components tick a now-marker and two routes read today.
Patience cannot be mistaken for a member on HttpClient.

Writing the rule and leaving the code alone was rejected, because a test cannot reach client.Timeout at all, so the rule would forbid the only thing the code made possible and the flaky tests would stay flaky.
Faking the stores and dropping the containers was rejected, because real Loki and real Tempo are where the queries, the day-by-day windowing and the answer parsing are proved.

Rewriting the four stand-ins with a faking library was rejected, because they already stand in for a store that is down, failing or never answers, and HttpMessageHandler.SendAsync is protected, the shape a faking library handles worst.

Writing the still Clock ourselves was rejected, because holding time still means a queue of pending timers fired in order, a concurrency primitive that is easily subtly wrong, and Microsoft ships one.
Keeping the word Timeout for the wait was rejected, because the rule forbids client.Timeout and the glossary word would sit one keystroke from the banned line.
One check that reads both languages as text was rejected, because C# written inside a string would be reported, so each language is held by the tool that parses it.
